title: Diagnosing floors and sills on a Simca Aronde
author: Caramagnols
excerpt: Before talking about paint or upholstery, an Aronde often demands a patient check of its base. Floors and sills quickly show whether the restoration will stay measured or not.
content:
A Simca Aronde can still look honest from a distance while its structure already calls for deep work. On this model, the floors, surrounding structural sections and sills often deliver the first serious verdict.

Begin with what the car hides best

Lower sections age away from view. Under tired carpets, doubled metal or a rapidly blackened underside, the real condition can remain invisible for a long time. That is why a serious diagnosis always begins with the base.

On an Aronde, one needs to inspect the continuity of the metal, the quality of earlier repairs, jacking points, sill joints and the way the doors sit in their openings.

Consider the signs before taking the car further apart

Even before dismantling, the car already speaks. A door that binds, a floor that sounds hollow, a confused weld or a body line that loses its clarity should all raise concern. Such signs do not by themselves price the job, but they do prevent illusions.

Dismantling then confirms the real extent. That is often the moment when a merely aged car becomes a structurally compromised one.

Why this diagnosis determines everything else

As long as the base is unclear, the rest of the budget stays vague. Paint, seals, trim or chrome make lasting sense only if the lower structure has become sound and coherent again.

In a serious restoration, diagnosing floors and sills is therefore not one stage among others. It is the condition that gives the rest of the project its true measure.
